overview: The Tunis entry covers a North African regency ruled by beys within the Ottoman political world. Its interval crosses Muradid rule and the Husainid dynasty established in 1705. Mosques, family houses, craftwork and nineteenth-century reforms reveal a society broader than its ruling household.

periods.title: Muradid rule and its aftermath
periods.summary: The seventeenth-century city acquired monumental buildings including Hammuda Pasha’s mosque.

periods.title: Husainid government
periods.summary: The Husainid dynasty established a long-lived ruling household in 1705.

periods.title: Reform and foreign pressure
periods.summary: The Fundamental Pact and constitution preceded the French protectorate imposed in 1881, after the map entry’s 1878 endpoint.

items.text: Hammuda Pasha’s mosque in Tunis is dated by an inscription to 1655. Its prayer hall measures about 24 by 17 metres and uses 48 columns to support its vaulted interior. Architecture supplies evidence for both religious life and organized building work.

The mosque joined worship with dynastic memory: Hammuda Pasha and his family were buried in a square mausoleum beside it. Green glazed roof tiles and contrasting marble decoration made the burial building conspicuous within the complex.

An eastern gallery included an outdoor prayer niche for summer worship. That small practical detail matters: a religious building also had to accommodate bodies, seasons and the need for usable space.

The 1861 constitution kept succession hereditary within the Husainid family, ordered by age. It also required two official registers recording the ruling family. Reform here meant defining and recording royal government, not immediately replacing monarchy with elected rule.

Dar Ben Abdallah is an eighteenth-century residence later made into a museum. Its reconstructed scenes focus on comfortable urban households of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. They are useful evidence for that social setting, not a model of every home in the regency.
The museum’s nineteenth-century room presents embroidery, belt weaving and chechia-cap knitting as women’s work. These were skilled activities producing things to wear, not merely decorative hobbies.

A childhood display shows a skilled embroiderer teaching two girls, alongside children’s clothes and toys. It offers a concrete example of knowledge being learned within household settings, while remaining a museum reconstruction.

The reconstructed kitchen occupies a small open courtyard, with sheltered areas for preparing food and cooking. Pottery, copper and wooden utensils show a kitchen assembled from several materials. The pots had jobs before they became museum exhibits.

Wedding displays include combs, mirrors, powder boxes, jewellery and clothing. These objects help explain preparations for a major family occasion; they do not establish one uniform wedding ceremony for all Tunisians.

A short Arabic sample from the 1857 Fundamental Pact is “اختلاف الأديان والألسنة والألوان”, meaning “differences of religions, languages and colours”. It appears within the first article’s promise of security for inhabitants regardless of these differences, reproduced here in typed Arabic from the ministry’s transcription.

The pact also addressed equality in taxation and customs duties, trading and work. These were promises about how government should treat people and property; the existence of a written guarantee alone does not prove equal treatment in everyday practice.

A dedicated archive service was created within the Grand Ministry in 1874. Preserving and organizing correspondence made government decisions retrievable. Behind a grand constitution stood the decidedly less glamorous but essential task of keeping the paperwork.

ending.text: The map entry ends in 1878, before a decisive change: France invaded and imposed the protectorate in 1881. The beys remained under colonial constraints, while Tunisia’s cities and communities continued into a different political order.
